newsitem.title: UK: Studies show your job affects your health.
newsitem.headline: Studies show your job affects your health.

text.p: A sheaf of reports published on Friday confirmed that what a person does for a living strongly influences how and when he or she will die.
They find that manual labourers, people with little control over their day-to-day jobs, those with high-stress jobs and poor people are all more likely to die from heart disease.
The reports in the British Medical Journal confirm earlier studies but cover large groups of people over decades of time.

George Davey Smith and a team at Britain's University of Bristol studied 5,700 men for 21 years and found manual workers born into working class families had a 70 percent higher chance of dying in any given year than non-manual workers.

Manual workers were more likely to smoke, have high blood pressure, be obese, and suffer from angina (chest pains) and bronchitis. "Health and risk of premature death are determined by socioeconomic factors acting throughout life," they wrote.

Heart disease was the biggest factor in their deaths. "Mortality from cardiovascular disease seems to be more strongly related to cumulative social disadvantage than does that from cancer or (other) causes," they added.

Hans Bosma of Erasmus University in Rotterdam, Netherlands and Michael Marmot and colleagues at University College Medical School in London found British civil servants were more likely to suffer coronary heart disease if they had little control over their jobs.
Their study of 10,000 government workers aged 35 to 55 found that having little say over what they did at work could cause the civil servants to develop heart disease.
"Men and women with low job control, either self-reported or independently assessed, had a higher risk of newly reported coronary heart disease," they wrote.

"This association could not be explained by employment grade, negative affectivity, or classic coronary risk factors. Job demands and social support at work were not related to the risk of coronary heart disease."
They said giving employees more variety and a stronger say in tasks could reduce such illnesses.
An earlier study by the same group found that male civil servants in lower grades had three times the risk of death from heart disease over 10 years than those in high grades.

Dr Caroline Morrison and colleagues of the Royal Infirmary in Glasgow studied more than 5,000 people aged 25 to 64 and found the more disadvantaged people were, the more likely they were to die from heart attacks.

Poorer people were less likely to be admitted to hospital for heart emergencies, and more likely to die outside hospital. Morrison asked whether doctors might treat poorer people differently but said other factors might be at work.
Finnish and U.S. researchers found that men with high job demands showed the most progression of atherosclerosis -- the clogging up of arteries that marks much heart disease.
Susan Everson of the Public health Institute in Berkeley, California studied nearly 600 Finnish men and found blood pressure and stress worked together to worsen atherosclerosis.
